Roadmap
Nine mental models. 185 concepts. The order is deliberate: each section
builds vocabulary you will use in the next.
01 Web, Networking & Delivery
Concepts 1-32: How a browser request finds a server, moves through infrastructure,
and gets data back.
02 Security, Identity & Trust
Concepts 33-47: The difference between knowing who someone is, deciding what
they can do, and protecting the path in between.
03 Databases & Data Integrity
Concepts 48-60: How persistent data stays fast, related, and correct when many
users act at once.
04 Realtime & Asynchronous JavaScript
Concepts 61-70: How JavaScript waits, streams, schedules, and communicates
without freezing the user experience.
05 JavaScript Core Mental Models
Concepts 71-90: The language behaviors that explain most "why did JavaScript do
THAT?" interview questions.
06 TypeScript & React
Concepts 91-117: The component, state, identity, and rendering concepts that
mid-level frontend interviews probe hardest.
07 Frontend Platform, UX & Performance
Concepts 118-140: How modern web apps load, render, navigate, stay accessible,
and feel fast.
08 Reliability, Architecture & Delivery
Concepts 141-170: How production software survives failure, grows in complexity,
and remains operable.
09 Computer Science & Engineering Judgment
Concepts 171-185: The compact mental models that turn syntax knowledge into
engineering judgment.

001 PLAIN WHY MEMORY REAL INTERVIEW 002 PLAIN WHY MEMORY REAL INTERVIEW 003 PLAIN WHY MEMORY REAL INTERVIEW 004 PLAIN WHY MEMORY REAL INTERVIEW 005 PLAIN WHY MEMORY REAL INTERVIEW HTTP
The request-response protocol used by browsers, apps, and servers to exchange web data.
It is the basic language behind APIs, pages, images, and most web traffic.
HTTP is a waiter: you order GET /pizza; the kitchen sends a response.
GET /users/42 -> 200 + JSON user data.
HTTP is a stateless request-response protocol. I use methods, headers, status codes, and bodies
to define the contract between client and server.
HTTPS
HTTP carried through TLS so traffic is encrypted and the server can prove its identity.
It protects credentials, tokens, and user data from easy interception or tampering.
HTTP is shouting your password across a cafe. HTTPS is whispering through a locked tube.
https://example.com/login encrypts the request while it travels over the network.
HTTPS is HTTP over TLS. TLS gives confidentiality, integrity, and server authentication.
TLS
A security protocol that establishes an encrypted, integrity-protected connection between peers.
It is what makes HTTPS trustworthy in transit.
Two spies agree on a secret code, then talk where everyone can hear but nobody can understand.
Browser verifies a certificate, negotiates keys, then sends encrypted HTTP.
TLS provides encryption, integrity, and authentication for network connections; HTTPS uses TLS
underneath.
DNS
The naming system that translates human-friendly domains into network addresses.
Users remember example.com, not server IP addresses.
DNS is your phone contacts: tap "Mum" instead of memorizing her number.
api.example.com -> an IP address returned by a DNS resolver.
DNS maps names to records such as IP addresses so clients can locate services.
IP address
A network address used to identify where packets should be delivered.
Networking needs an addressable destination for hosts and interfaces.
The IP is the apartment building address; you still need the port to find the right door.
192.168.1.20 is a private IPv4 address; IPv6 uses a larger address space.
An IP address identifies a network endpoint. Applications usually reach it indirectly through DNS.

010 PLAIN WHY MEMORY REAL INTERVIEW HTTP status codes
Three-digit codes that summarize the outcome of an HTTP response.
They let clients handle success, redirects, client errors, and server errors consistently.
A restaurant scorecard: 2xx "here is dinner", 4xx "you ordered nonsense", 5xx "the kitchen is on
fire".
200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content, 400 Bad Request, 401, 403, 404, 409, 429, 500, 503.
I treat 2xx as success, 4xx as client-side request/auth issues, and 5xx as server-side failures;
specific codes matter for client behavior.
011 PLAIN WHY MEMORY REAL INTERVIEW Headers
Metadata fields attached to HTTP requests and responses.
They carry information such as content type, authorization, caching rules, and tracing IDs.
The parcel label is not the gift; it says what is inside and where it should go.
Authorization: Bearer ..., Content-Type: application/json, Cache-Control: max-age=3600.
Headers carry protocol metadata separate from the main payload, for example auth, caching,
content negotiation, and correlation IDs.
012 Request body
PLAIN The payload sent inside a request, commonly with POST, PUT, or PATCH.
WHY It transports structured input that does not belong in the URL.
MEMORY The envelope is the request; the letter inside is the body.
REAL POST /users body: {"name":"Ada","email":"a@example.com"}.
INTERVIEW The request body contains payload data, typically JSON or form data, for operations that create or
modify resources.
013 Query parameters
PLAIN Key-value values appended to a URL after ? to alter how a resource is retrieved.
WHY They are convenient for filtering, sorting, searching, and pagination.
MEMORY You order "pizza?size=large&spicy=true" instead of inventing a new pizza endpoint.
REAL GET /products?category=laptops&page=2&sort=price.
INTERVIEW I use query parameters for optional modifiers such as filters, sort order, search terms, and
pagination.

014 PLAIN WHY MEMORY REAL INTERVIEW Path parameter
A dynamic segment in a URL path used to identify a specific resource or nested location.
It gives stable, readable resource addresses.
/dogs/fluffy means "the dog named Fluffy", not "all dogs with ?dog=fluffy".
GET /users/42 where 42 is the user ID.
Path parameters usually identify a concrete resource, while query parameters usually modify how
a collection is retrieved.
015 PLAIN WHY MEMORY REAL INTERVIEW REST API
An API style centered on resources, standard HTTP semantics, stateless requests, and
representations.
It gives teams a predictable way to design web APIs.
A library has /books/42, not /pleaseGiveMeBookNumber42Now.
GET /users/42, PATCH /users/42, DELETE /users/42.
REST models resources and uses HTTP semantics consistently. I focus more on clear resource
contracts than on blindly following naming rules.
016 PLAIN WHY MEMORY REAL INTERVIEW API
A defined interface through which software components communicate.
It separates implementation details from the contract consumers rely on.
A vending machine exposes buttons and a coin slot; you do not need to know its internal gears.
Frontend calls /api/orders; a payment service exposes a create-payment API.
An API is a contract between software components. Web APIs often use HTTP, but APIs can also be

A system whose behavior depends on state remembered across interactions.

user role can read reports; admin role can delete accounts.

authenticated request.

048 PLAIN WHY MEMORY REAL INTERVIEW Database
A system for persistently storing, querying, and updating application data.
Applications need durable state that survives process restarts.
Your app's memory is a goldfish; the database is the notebook it writes everything into.
Orders, users, and payments live in PostgreSQL instead of a Node process variable.
A database provides durable storage plus query/update mechanisms and consistency guarantees
appropriate to its model.
049 PLAIN WHY MEMORY REAL INTERVIEW Relational database
A database model built around tables, rows, columns, relationships, and constraints.
It is excellent when data relationships and transactional consistency matter.
A very strict spreadsheet where rows can point to rows in other sheets and rules stop nonsense.
PostgreSQL tables users and orders linked by orders.user_id.
Relational databases model structured data with tables and constraints and are queried
commonly with SQL; they are strong for transactional workloads.
050 PLAIN WHY MEMORY REAL INTERVIEW Primary key
A column or column set that uniquely identifies each row in a table.
Other rows and indexes need a stable identity for each record.
Every student gets a unique school number even if three students are named Alex.
users.id is PRIMARY KEY; each value is unique and non-null.
A primary key uniquely identifies a row and is the natural target for foreign-key references.
051 Foreign key
PLAIN A constraint linking a value in one table to a key in another table.
WHY It protects referential integrity between related records.
MEMORY A library loan card cannot reference book ID 999 if book 999 does not exist.
REAL orders.user_id REFERENCES users(id).
INTERVIEW A foreign key enforces that a relationship points to a valid referenced row, unless nullability or
cascading rules say otherwise.
052 PLAIN WHY MEMORY REAL INTERVIEW Database index
A data structure maintained to make particular lookups or orderings faster.
Without useful indexes, large queries may scan huge numbers of rows.
The index at the back of a cookbook lets you jump to "pasta" instead of reading every page.
CREATE INDEX idx_users_email ON users(email); speeds email lookups.
Indexes trade additional storage and write cost for faster reads. I design them around actual
query patterns and verify with query plans.

053 PLAIN WHY MEMORY REAL INTERVIEW 054 PLAIN WHY MEMORY REAL INTERVIEW 055 PLAIN WHY MEMORY REAL INTERVIEW 056 PLAIN WHY MEMORY REAL INTERVIEW SQL JOIN
An operation that combines rows from related tables based on a condition.
Normalized relational data is intentionally split across tables and must often be recombined when
queried.
You match a pile of name tags with a pile of lunch orders using the same student ID.
SELECT u.name,o.total FROM users u JOIN orders o ON u.id=o.user_id.
JOINs combine related rows. I know INNER JOIN for matching rows and LEFT JOIN when I need all
left-side rows even without matches.
Transaction
A group of database operations treated as a single logical unit that commits or rolls back.
It prevents partial updates that would leave business data inconsistent.
Moving a cake: either the whole cake reaches the table or we pretend the move never happened;
half a cake is not a valid transaction.
Debit account A and credit account B inside BEGIN...COMMIT; on failure ROLLBACK.
Transactions make related writes atomic and provide isolation guarantees so partial business
operations are not persisted.
ACID
A mnemonic for transaction properties: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability.
It summarizes the guarantees expected from robust transactional databases.
A = all-or-nothing; C = rules stay sane; I = shoppers do not trample each other; D = the receipt
survives a power cut.
A committed order survives restart; concurrent updates respect the chosen isolation level.
ACID describes transactional guarantees. I pay particular attention to isolation level and business
invariants rather than treating the acronym as magic.
Race condition
A bug where correctness depends on the unpredictable timing/interleaving of concurrent
operations.
Concurrent requests can both make decisions from stale state.
Two people see the last donut, both shout "mine", and both somehow leave with a donut receipt.
Stock=1; requests A and B both read 1 before either decrements. Use transaction/locking/atomic
update.
A race condition occurs when concurrent operations access shared state without sufficient
coordination. I fix the invariant, not just add random delays.

A concurrency strategy that allows reads freely but rejects an update if the record changed since
it was read.
It avoids heavy locks when conflicts are uncommon.
You edit a shared document version 7; if someone already saved version 8, your version 7 save is
rejected.
UPDATE docs SET ..., version=8 WHERE id=1 AND version=7; zero rows means conflict.
Optimistic locking detects conflicts using a version/timestamp and asks the caller to retry or
resolve when concurrent changes occur.

A long-lived full-duplex connection that lets client and server send messages in both directions.
It is useful when both sides need low-latency real-time communication.
HTTP is sending letters; WebSocket is keeping a phone call open.
Chat client and server continuously exchange messages over one connection.

both need to push events, while planning reconnects and scaling connection state.
062 Polling
PLAIN Repeatedly requesting the latest state on a timer.
WHY It is simple and reliable when a few seconds of delay is acceptable.
MEMORY Every five seconds you ask the oven, "Are we there yet?"
REAL setInterval(() => fetch("/status"), 5000).

backoff/visibility awareness to avoid waste.

A long-lived HTTP connection where the server continuously pushes text events to the browser in
one direction.

AI token stream or live job progress delivered through EventSource/SSE.

it is great for feeds and progress where client messages can use normal HTTP.

It replaces wasteful polling for external service events.

JavaScript declaration forms with different scoping and reassignment behavior.
Choosing predictable declarations reduces bugs and communicates intent.
const is "do not replace this box"; let is "this label may point somewhere else"; var is the weird

JavaScript's declaration processing behavior that makes some bindings/functions known before

083 PLAIN WHY MEMORY Array.map
An array method that creates a new array by transforming each element.
It is the natural tool when input and output have one item per item.
Every potato walks through a machine and becomes a french fry; nobody is removed.
REAL [1,2,3].map(n=>n*2) -> [2,4,6].
INTERVIEW map transforms every element and returns a new array of the same length. I use it frequently to
transform data and render lists.
084 PLAIN WHY MEMORY Array.filter
An array method that creates a new array containing only elements that pass a predicate.
It expresses selection without manual loops and mutation.
A nightclub bouncer lets only people with valid tickets into the new array.
REAL users.filter(u=>u.active).
INTERVIEW filter keeps the elements whose predicate returns truthy; output length can be smaller than input.
085 PLAIN WHY MEMORY Array.find
An array method that returns the first element matching a predicate, or undefined.
It avoids scanning manually when only one match is needed.
Search the sock drawer and stop as soon as you find the first red sock.
REAL users.find(u=>u.id===42).
INTERVIEW find returns the first matching element, unlike filter which returns all matches in a new array.

An array method that returns whether at least one element passes a predicate.
It expresses existential checks clearly and short-circuits once true.
Do we have at least one slice of pizza left? If yes, stop counting.

INTERVIEW some answers "does any item match?" and returns a boolean, short-circuiting when it finds a
match.

Are all penguins wearing their tiny helmets? One missing helmet makes the answer false.

JavaScript plus a static type system checked before runtime.
It catches many integration mistakes earlier and documents contracts for humans and tools.
JavaScript lets you put soup in a USB port; TypeScript yells before you try.
function add(a:number,b:number):number { return a+b; }

A TypeScript declaration describing the expected shape/capabilities of an object or class.
It makes contracts explicit and reusable.
A job description says "must have id and name" without caring who the employee is.
interface User { id:number; name:string }
An interface describes a structural contract. TypeScript is structurally typed, so compatible
shapes can satisfy the interface.
Union type
A type that allows a value to be one of several alternatives.
It models finite UI states and domain choices safely.
The traffic light can be "red" | "amber" | "green" and not "banana".
type Status = "loading" | "success" | "error".
Union types model alternatives. Combined with discriminated unions, they make impossible
states harder to represent.
Generic
A type parameter that lets code stay reusable while preserving type information.
It avoids giving up safety with any when logic should work across types.
A labeled reusable box: Box<T> works for books, socks, or dragons while still remembering what
is inside.
function first<T>(xs:T[]):T|undefined { return xs[0]; }

A reusable unit that describes UI from props, state, and context.

A Lego instruction booklet for one UI piece: give it data, it tells React what that piece should look

storing values that can be derived.

Attempting a failed operation again when the failure may be temporary.
Transient network/service errors often succeed later.

Exponential backoff
A retry strategy where delays grow after consecutive failures, often with random jitter.
It gives a recovering service breathing room and avoids synchronized retry storms.
Knock again after 1s, then 2s, then 4s - do not machine-gun the doorbell.
Retry delays 500ms, 1s, 2s, 4s plus random jitter.
Exponential backoff reduces pressure during outages; jitter prevents many clients from retrying in

The property that repeating an operation has the same intended effect as performing it once.
Networks retry, users double-click, and clients time out after servers already committed work.

charging twice.
Idempotency makes retries safe. I use idempotency keys or natural resource semantics for
operations that must not duplicate side effects.

them later.
It decouples request latency from background work and smooths bursts.

The component or resource that currently limits overall system performance.
Optimizing non-bottlenecks does not meaningfully improve the system.
If the doorway fits one person, buying faster shoes for everyone does not fix the queue.

170 PLAIN WHY MEMORY REAL INTERVIEW N+1 query problem
A data-access pattern where one initial query is followed by one additional query per returned

175 Queue
PLAIN A First-In-First-Out data structure.
WHY It models ordered work waiting to be processed.
MEMORY Supermarket line: first person in line should be served first unless chaos has won.
REAL Job queue, BFS frontier, request buffer.
INTERVIEW A queue is FIFO: enqueue at the back, dequeue from the front. It is foundational for scheduling
and breadth-first traversal.
176 PLAIN WHY MEMORY REAL INTERVIEW Recursion
A function or algorithm solving a problem by calling itself on a smaller subproblem until a base
case.
It maps naturally to trees and divide-and-conquer problems.
Russian nesting dolls: open one doll, find a smaller doll, stop when there is no smaller doll.
factorial(n) returns n * factorial(n-1) with base case n<=1.
Recursion needs a base case and progress toward it. I also consider stack depth and iterative
alternatives for large inputs.
177 PLAIN WHY MEMORY REAL INTERVIEW Memory leak
Memory that remains reachable/retained even though the application no longer needs it.
Long-running apps can become slower or crash as retained memory accumulates.
You keep every takeaway container forever because one tiny string is still tied to each box.
Forgotten event listener closes over a large object after component cleanup should have removed
it.
In garbage-collected JavaScript, leaks usually mean unwanted references keep objects reachable.
I investigate heap growth, listeners, timers, caches, and closures.
178 PLAIN WHY MEMORY REAL INTERVIEW Garbage collection
Automatic runtime reclamation of memory for objects that are no longer reachable.
JavaScript developers do not manually free most memory, but must avoid retaining unnecessary
references.
The cleaner removes abandoned boxes only when nobody still has a string tied to them.
An object with no reachable references becomes eligible for collection.
Garbage collection reclaims unreachable memory automatically; it does not prevent leaks caused
by objects that remain reachable accidentally.

179 PLAIN WHY MEMORY REAL INTERVIEW Deep equality vs reference equality
Reference equality checks whether two object references point to the same object; deep equality
compares nested contents.
React and memoization often care about identity rather than structural sameness.
Two identical-looking twins are not the same person; one person viewed through two windows is
the same person.
{} === {} is false; const b=a; a===b is true.
JavaScript === compares object identity, not deep structure. New object literals are different
references even if contents are identical.
180 PLAIN WHY MEMORY REAL INTERVIEW Pure function
A function whose output depends only on its inputs and that produces no observable side effects.
Pure logic is easier to test, cache, parallelize, and reason about.
A calculator gives 2+3=5 every time and does not secretly order pizza while calculating.
function add(a,b){ return a+b; }.
Pure functions are deterministic and side-effect free for the same inputs. I keep domain
calculations pure where practical.
181 PLAIN WHY MEMORY Side effect
An observable interaction outside a function's returned value, such as I/O, mutation, logging,
timers, or DOM changes.
Effects are necessary but should be made explicit and controlled.
A function that returns 5 and also paints your wall blue has a side effect.
REAL fetch(), localStorage.setItem(), console.log(), document.title=...
INTERVIEW Side effects interact with external state. I isolate them at boundaries so core logic remains easier
to test and reason about.
182 PLAIN WHY MEMORY REAL INTERVIEW DRY
Don't Repeat Yourself: avoid duplicating the same knowledge or rule in multiple places.
Duplicated business rules drift and make maintenance risky.
Do not keep the same phone number written on 17 sticky notes if changing it requires a treasure
hunt.
Centralize one tax calculation used by checkout and invoice instead of copying it twice.
DRY is about duplicated knowledge, not eliminating every repeated line. I prefer a little
duplication over a wrong premature abstraction.

183 PLAIN WHY MEMORY REAL INTERVIEW KISS
Keep It Simple: prefer the simplest design that correctly satisfies current requirements.
Simple systems are easier to understand, test, operate, and change.
Do not build a satellite to pass the salt across the dinner table.
Use one clear service and database before introducing a distributed event mesh for 20 users.
KISS means minimizing accidental complexity while still meeting correctness, reliability, and
maintainability needs.
184 PLAIN WHY MEMORY REAL INTERVIEW YAGNI
You Aren't Gonna Need It: do not build speculative features or architecture without a real
requirement.
Unused flexibility creates code, tests, failure modes, and maintenance cost today.
Do not install a shark tank in your apartment because maybe one day you will own a shark.
Do not introduce Kubernetes for a single small service solely because traffic might explode
someday.
YAGNI pushes me to solve evidenced requirements and leave clean extension points instead of
implementing hypothetical future systems.
185 PLAIN WHY MEMORY REAL INTERVIEW Technical debt
Future engineering cost created by shortcuts, outdated design, or deliberate trade-offs in today's
implementation.
Debt can accelerate delivery, but unmanaged debt compounds and slows future change.
Borrow 10 minutes by stuffing everything in a closet; tomorrow you may spend an hour finding
your shoes.
Ship a manual workflow for launch, document the constraint, add telemetry, schedule
replacement when volume proves need.
Technical debt is not automatically bad. I make trade-offs explicit, understand interest/risk, and
prioritize repayment based on product impact.
